title: Your Library App Is Adding an AI Content Filter — Sort Of
hook: Libby, the library ebook app, is letting readers hide AI-generated books, narration, and art. The catch: the filter only works if publishers and authors honestly disclose using AI.
key_points: Libby (from OverDrive) is rolling out settings to show or hide AI-generated content.
It covers AI authorship, AI-narrated audiobooks, machine translation, and AI-generated art.
OverDrive isn't excluding AI-made titles from the catalog — it's asking publishers to self-identify them.
The filter's accuracy depends entirely on that self-disclosure being honest.
New OverDrive CEO Marc DeBevoise: 'We need to tell people what's available [and] how it was created.'
content_html: Digital libraries are quietly becoming a new front in the AI-content debate. The Verge reports that Libby, the ebook and audiobook app used by libraries everywhere, is rolling out settings that let readers choose whether they want to see AI-generated content at all — covering AI-written text, AI-narrated audiobooks, machine translation, and AI-generated cover art.
extra_html: New OverDrive CEO Marc DeBevoise frames the move plainly: "We need to tell people what's available [and] how it was created." But the mechanism has a real gap. OverDrive isn't independently detecting AI content — it's asking publishers and self-published authors to disclose it themselves, and the filter only works as well as that disclosure is honest. A publisher that skips the label, intentionally or not, slips past the filter entirely. It's the same trade-off that shows up across AI content moderation: a labeling system built on trust is better than nothing, but it's not proof, and readers who care should treat an "AI-free" filter as a helpful signal rather than a guarantee.

related.title: Spotting AI-Made Content
related.hook: There are real tells for AI text and images — but they're fading fast, and 'AI detector' tools are unreliable. The durable skill is judging the source, not squinting at the pixels.

related.title: AI 'Creators' Are Getting Harder to Spot
related.hook: AI influencers used to be easy to clock — too-smooth skin, an uncanny stare. The tells are vanishing, and fully synthetic 'creators' now slip into feeds without announcing themselves.

flashcards.prompt: How does Libby's new AI content filter actually work?

choices.text: Publishers and authors self-disclose AI use, and readers can then choose to hide it
An AI model automatically scans every book and detects AI content with certainty
It removes all AI-assisted books from the catalog entirely

flashcards.explanation_html: OverDrive relies on publishers and self-published authors to label their own AI use — it doesn't run independent detection on every title.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the filter's usefulness limited, even though it sounds helpful?
flashcards.back_html: It only catches what's honestly self-disclosed — an author who doesn't label their AI use won't be flagged, so the filter can't be fully trusted.
